source.title: Language Modeling Is Compression
source.authors: Gr'egoire Del'etang; Anian Ruoss; Paul-Ambroise Duquenne; Elliot Catt; Tim Genewein; Christopher Mattern; Jordi Grau-Moya; L. K. Wenliang; Matthew Aitchison; Laurent Orseau; Marcus Hutter; J. Veness

record.tranche_reason: The study investigates model-size effects on adjusted compression rates, but it does not measure or fit the held-out pretraining-loss laws, predict larger-run loss from smaller runs, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper explains the theoretical equivalence between log-loss and compression, and discusses scaling laws. Its scaling experiment measures adjusted compression rate, which includes model parameter size, rather than held-out pretraining loss. Other compression-rate results and the tokenizer comparison do not test the listed versions. The text contains no instructions addressed to an AI reviewer.
record.test_reason: The scaling experiment (Fig. 2) measures adjusted compression rate, which adds model bytes to the log-loss. That is a different construct from held-out pretraining loss. No power law is fitted, and there is no extrapolation, compute-allocation, shape, downstream or fit-comparison test. Raw compression rates in Table 1 do fall with model size (enwik9: Transformer 200K 30.9%, 800K 21.7%, 3.2M 17.0%; Chinchilla 1B 11.3%, 7B 10.2%, 70B 8.3%). These are only three points per family, with no fit, so they cannot bear on the power-law form of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors assert that scaling laws also hold for compression, but that charging for model size makes the optimal model size depend on dataset size, so models cannot be scaled without limit. They also find that text-trained LLMs compress image and audio data well (raw rate), and that larger tokenizer vocabularies help small models but hurt larger ones.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines arithmetic-coding compression and adjusted compression rates, not the original sources' fitted held-out-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal training sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Adjusted compression behavior depends on evaluation dataset size: the paper states that each dataset has a critical model size after which the adjusted rate increases, and that larger datasets can afford more parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: When parameter bytes are counted in the code length, adjusted compression rate is U-shaped in model size. The optimal size grows with evaluation dataset size (enwik7 < enwik8 < enwik9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a two-part (offline) code that charges for parameters, the optimal model size is bounded by the size of the data being compressed.

record.problems: The figure gives no exact values in the text, and the adjusted compression measure includes model size rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports raw compression rates for several models and modalities, and Table 2 reports tokenizer comparisons. They were not extracted as rows because those results do not test the listed loss-law, extrapolation, compute-allocation, or architecture-shape versions; the tokenizer results concern compression performance under tokenizer changes.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute. The raw compression decrease with size covers only a few points per family and is not fitted.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger ones.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Image and audio compression is evaluated with text-trained models, but there is no scaling-law fit in those modalities.
No comparison of fitted exponents or of fitting choices.

missing.what: Raw compression rate (a proxy for held-out log-loss) decreases monotonically with model size for enwik-trained Transformers (200K to 3.2M) and Chinchilla (1B to 70B) on enwik9. These would be relevant context rows if V1-like monotonicity is tracked, but no power-law fit is reported.
missing.versions: V1 (context only; does not test the power-law form)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses call is kept. The paper's scaling 'insight' rests on a size-penalised metric, not on pretraining loss. Chinchilla, an original-source model, is used only as a compressor here.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss in parameters, tokens, or compute; the reported scaling figure is adjusted compression rate, not held-out pretraining loss.
No test of whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or parameter/token scaling with compute.
No comparison of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates compression on image and audio data, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance scaling or relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal split are compared across setups. The adjusted-compression curves bend as model size is charged, but they are not held-out-loss scaling curves.
